subtitulo: Bargaining is a friendly ritual at a craft market and completely out of place at a fixed-price shop — knowing which one you're in is the whole skill
cena: The price the vendor just said out loud was clearly an opening move, not a final number — and how you respond in the next ten seconds decides whether this turns into a game or an insult.
decisao: aceitar o primeiro preço ou negociar — ler se a banca é de preço aberto ou fixo decide se você paga trinta por cento a mais ou passa vergonha tentando regatear no supermercado
frasePiso: Bargaining is a conversation, not a fight — and knowing where it belongs is worth more than knowing how to do it.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: Bargaining is socially accepted and often expected at informal markets like a tianguis or craft market, especially where prices aren't marked, but it is uncommon and generally not attempted at fixed shops, chain stores or supermarkets.
fatosDatados.fonte: Consenso de guias culturais (Baconismagic, Where Sidewalks End, Sand In My Suitcase)

fatosDatados.afirmacao: A common pattern in market bargaining is to expect to pay somewhat less than the initial asking price, often reported around 30 percent off, achieved through friendly, respectful negotiation rather than aggressive pressure.
fatosDatados.fonte: Consenso de guias culturais (Sand In My Suitcase; Where Sidewalks End)

steps.pt: Today's real skill isn't the phrases — it's knowing where they belong. Get that right and the rest is easy.
I'll give you this one for five hundred.
A craft stall with no price tag or register is an invitation to negotiate — a supermarket isn't. Read the room first.

steps.promptPt: You're at an open craft stall, no price marked. Ask a friendly opening question. Speak now.

steps.pt: I'll let it go for four hundred.
Now counter-offer, friendly not aggressive — a conversation, not a demand. Genuine interest gets you further than pressure.

steps.promptPt: Offer a lower price, warmly. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Se lo puedo dejar en trescientos cincuenta?
steps.pinyin: seh loh PWEH-doh deh-HAR en trehs-syen-tohs seen-KWEN-tah
steps.pt: Could I offer three hundred fifty?
steps.tts: ¿Se lo puedo dejar en trescientos cincuenta?

steps.pt: A friendly back-and-forth commonly lands around thirty percent off the opening price — not a rule, just a rough shape.

steps.promptPt: Many stalls like this run cash-only. Confirm before you dig for a card. Speak now.
steps.pt: Can I pay you in cash?
If the answer is a flat no, that's the end of it — pushing further sours the exchange. Thank them either way.

steps.promptPt: The vendor can't go any lower. Thank them warmly, whether or not you buy. Speak now.
steps.pt: That's fine, thank you very much.

steps.promptPt: Point and quantify, nothing else. Speak now.
steps.pt: Can I have two of those?

steps.promptPt: Volume is the honest way into a better price. Speak now.
steps.pt: Is there a discount if I take two?

steps.promptPt: Ask about the stall, not about this piece. Speak now.
It is a gift and it has to survive the flight. Speak now.
steps.pt: Can you wrap it for me?

aprofundar.titulo: Bargaining is a genre, not a universal rule

secoes.corpo: No price tag, no register, an open-air or craft market stall — these signal that negotiation is expected. A fixed shop, chain store or supermarket does not work this way, and attempting to bargain there is simply out of place.
A warm tone, a smile and genuine interest in the item get better results than pressure. The vendor is a person having a normal workday, not an opponent.
If the seller won't move on price, pushing further is the one thing that damages the interaction. Accept it gracefully — you can still buy at the stated price, or simply thank them and move on.

permissao: You are allowed to just pay the asking price if bargaining doesn't feel comfortable. Negotiating well is a nice skill, but declining to haggle and paying what's asked is never rude — the discomfort is yours to manage, not a social obligation.
espelho: Anyone who's ever negotiated at a garage sale or a flea market back home already knows this exact rhythm — friendly opening question, a counter-offer, a graceful acceptance of 'no' — the only new part is which settings it applies to here.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You try to negotiate the price at a supermarket checkout or a branded clothing store, and the cashier looks confused rather than engaged.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: Bargaining doesn't work here at all, or this cashier is just unfriendly.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Bargaining is a specific ritual belonging to informal settings — open-air markets, craft stalls, tianguis — not a general rule for every purchase in Mexico; fixed-price retail simply isn't the context it applies to.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Save negotiation for stalls without visible price tags or registers, and pay the stated price at any fixed shop without hesitation.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You avoid an awkward, mismatched interaction and reserve the fun, friendly haggling for the settings where it's actually expected and enjoyed.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: This ficha itself is about knowing where NOT to bargain — the exception is the informal market setting covered in the main lesson, where the opposite applies.
